questions.stem: Using collision theory, which statement describes a chemical system at dynamic equilibrium?
options: Successful collisions occur at the same rate in the forward and reverse directions
Collisions between reactant particles stop once the products have formed
Only collisions between product particles continue at equilibrium
Successful collisions occur in the forward direction only, but more slowly
questions.explanation: At equilibrium both reactions continue, and the rate of successful forward collisions equals the rate of successful reverse collisions. Collisions never stop; particles keep reacting in both directions, which is why the equilibrium is called dynamic.

questions.stem: Why do macroscopic properties such as colour and pressure stay constant in a system at equilibrium?
options: The temperature of the system falls until no particle has enough energy to react
Each substance is formed as fast as it is used up, so its concentration is constant
All the particles have stopped reacting, so no further change can take place
The reactants and products are present at exactly equal concentrations
questions.explanation: Because the forward and reverse rates are equal, every substance is produced at the same rate as it is consumed, so its concentration, and the properties that depend on it, do not change. The concentrations are constant but need not be equal to each other.

questions.stem: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O. Adding concentrated hydrochloric acid turns a pink solution blue, and adding water turns it pink again. What does this demonstrate?
options: The reaction is irreversible once the blue complex has formed
Water and chloride ions act as catalysts for the colour change
Hydrochloric acid permanently converts the cobalt ions to a new metal
The reaction is reversible and can be driven in either direction
questions.explanation: Adding chloride ions favours the forward reaction (blue), and adding water favours the reverse reaction (pink). Because the change can be pushed back and forth, the reaction is reversible; neither substance is acting as a catalyst, since each is a reactant or product in the equation.

questions.stem: To model equilibrium, water is transferred back and forth between two measuring cylinders with tubes of different widths. After many transfers the water levels stop changing, though transfers continue. What do the constant levels represent?
options: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped
The reactants have been completely converted to products
The amounts of reactants and products have become equal
The forward and reverse rates have become equal
questions.explanation: Each transfer represents a reaction, and the levels stop changing when the volume moved each way per transfer is the same, just as concentrations stop changing when forward and reverse rates are equal. Transfers continue, which models the dynamic nature of equilibrium.

questions.stem: In the measuring cylinder model of equilibrium, the final water levels in the two cylinders are unequal. What does this feature of the model show about real equilibrium systems?
options: Equilibrium is reached only when the reverse reaction has stopped
The forward rate stays greater than the reverse rate at equilibrium
Equilibrium can be reached only if the system is open to the air
Equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products need not be equal
questions.explanation: Unequal final volumes correspond to unequal equilibrium concentrations: the position of equilibrium depends on the reaction, not on making amounts equal. What is equal at equilibrium is the rate of the forward and reverse processes, shown in the model by equal volumes transferred each way.

questions.stem: Why can a dynamic equilibrium be established only in a closed system?
options: A closed system forces the reactants and products to reach equal amounts
Products cannot escape, so the reverse reaction can occur as fast as the forward one
A closed system keeps the temperature low enough for both reactions to stop
Energy cannot leave a closed system, so the reaction cannot be exothermic
questions.explanation: In an open system a product such as a gas can escape, so it is not available to react in the reverse direction and the forward reaction continues until a reactant runs out. In a closed system no matter enters or leaves, so the reverse rate can rise until it matches the forward rate.

questions.stem: In a sealed bottle of soft drink, CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) is at equilibrium. Why does the drink go flat after the bottle is left open?
options: Air entering the bottle reacts with the dissolved CO₂ and destroys it
The equilibrium constant falls to zero as soon as the cap is removed
CO₂ gas escapes, so the system is open and dissolved CO₂ keeps leaving
Opening the bottle raises the pressure, which pushes CO₂ into solution
questions.explanation: Once the bottle is open, gaseous CO₂ escapes, lowering its concentration above the liquid; the system shifts towards CO₂(g) and, because the gas keeps escaping, equilibrium is never re-established. The value of Keq depends only on temperature, so opening the bottle does not change it.

questions.stem: Pure N₂O₄ is sealed in a flask and N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) begins. How do the forward and reverse rates change until equilibrium is reached?
options: Both rates rise steadily together from zero until the reactant is used up completely
The forward rate stays constant while the reverse rate rises until it exceeds the forward rate
The forward rate falls from its maximum and the reverse rate rises from zero until they are equal
The forward rate rises from zero and the reverse rate falls from its maximum until they are equal
questions.explanation: At the start only N₂O₄ is present, so the forward rate is greatest and the reverse rate is zero. As N₂O₄ is used up and NO₂ builds up, the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two rates are equal, which defines equilibrium.

questions.stem: A little radioactive iodine, I₂*, is added to an equilibrium mixture of H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). No macroscopic change is seen, but radioactive atoms are soon found in the HI. What does this show?
options: The added iodine has shifted the equilibrium completely to HI
The radioactive iodine has catalysed the formation of extra HI
The reverse reaction stops as soon as equilibrium is reached
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Radioactive atoms can only end up in HI if HI keeps forming, and HI must also keep decomposing for the concentrations to stay constant. This tracer experiment is evidence that equilibrium is dynamic; a small addition of I₂ would shift the position only slightly, not completely.

questions.stem: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the system:
options: adjusts to partially counteract the change and re-establish equilibrium
adjusts to fully reverse the change and return to the original concentrations
stops reacting until the disturbance is removed from the system
shifts to increase the effect of the change on the system
questions.explanation: The system shifts in the direction that partly opposes the disturbance, then settles at a new equilibrium. It does not fully undo the change: for example, after a reactant is added its new equilibrium concentration is still higher than before.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is at equilibrium. More O₂ is added at constant volume and temperature. Compared with the original equilibrium, the O₂ concentration at the new equilibrium is:
options: higher than originally, but lower than just after the addition
equal to the original value, because the change is fully reversed
lower than originally, because O₂ is used to make extra SO₃
equal to the value just after the addition, because K is constant
questions.explanation: The system shifts right, using up some of the added O₂ to make SO₃, so the O₂ concentration falls from its value just after the addition. Le Chatelier's principle predicts only partial opposition, so the new O₂ concentration remains above the original.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ammonia is removed by liquefying it as the gas mixture cools. How does this increase the yield?
options: Removing ammonia stops the forward reaction from being exothermic
Lowering [NH₃] makes the system shift right to replace it
Lowering [NH₃] increases the value of Keq for the reaction
Cooling the gas speeds up the forward reaction more than any other change
questions.explanation: Removing a product lowers its concentration, so the system shifts right to partly replace it, converting more nitrogen and hydrogen. Keq is unchanged because the temperature of the reaction vessel is unchanged; only the position of equilibrium moves.

questions.stem: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) is at equilibrium. Immediately after extra Fe³⁺ is added, which statement is correct?
options: Both rates increase by the same amount, so the position does not change
The forward rate falls, because the added ions get in the way of collisions
Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ collide more often, so the forward rate exceeds the reverse rate
FeSCN²⁺ ions collide more often, so the reverse rate exceeds the forward rate
questions.explanation: A higher Fe³⁺ concentration makes collisions between Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ more frequent, so the forward rate rises while the reverse rate is at first unchanged. The net forward reaction raises [FeSCN²⁺] until the rates are equal again, so the solution becomes a deeper red.

questions.stem: For an equilibrium whose forward reaction is exothermic, the temperature is increased. Using collision theory, what happens?
options: Both rates increase, but the reverse rate increases more
Both rates increase, but the forward rate increases more
The forward rate increases and the reverse rate decreases
Both rates decrease, but the forward rate decreases more
questions.explanation: Heating gives more particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy in both directions. The endothermic direction, here the reverse, has the larger activation energy and its rate rises by a greater factor, so the equilibrium shifts left, absorbing some of the added heat.

questions.stem: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O. A purple equilibrium mixture turns blue in hot water and pink in ice water. What can be concluded?
options: The forward reaction is exothermic
Heating removes water from the system
Cooling adds chloride ions to the system
The forward reaction is endothermic
questions.explanation: Heating shifts an equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which absorbs heat. The mixture turns blue when heated, so the forward reaction to [CoCl₄]²⁻ is endothermic, and cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction. No substance is added or removed by heating or cooling a sealed mixture.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is at equilibrium in a sealed syringe. The volume is decreased at constant temperature. What happens to the position of equilibrium?
options: It shifts left, towards more gas particles
It does not shift, as the temperature is constant
It shifts left, because the products are compressed
It shifts right, towards fewer gas particles
questions.explanation: Decreasing the volume increases the total pressure. The system partly counteracts this by shifting towards the side with fewer moles of gas: 2 mol of SO₃ on the right compared with 3 mol of gas on the left.

questions.stem: The volume of 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at equilibrium is halved. Using collision theory, why does the equilibrium shift to the right?
options: Every concentration doubles, and the reverse rate, which involves two gas particles, rises more
The particles move faster in the smaller volume, so more collisions exceed the activation energy
Only the reactant concentrations increase, because the products are compressed into a liquid
Every concentration doubles, and the forward rate, which involves three gas particles, rises more
questions.explanation: Halving the volume doubles every concentration, so collisions increase in both directions. The forward reaction involves three reactant gas particles and the reverse only two, so the forward collision rate rises by a larger factor until a new equilibrium is reached. Particle speed depends on temperature, which has not changed.

questions.stem: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g) is at equilibrium. The volume of the vessel is halved at constant temperature. What happens?
options: The position shifts right, because pressure favours the products
The position shifts left, because pressure favours the reactants
All concentrations stay the same and the pressure does not change
All concentrations double and the position of equilibrium does not shift
questions.explanation: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so a pressure change cannot be counteracted by a shift and Q remains equal to Keq. The concentrations of all four gases double because the same amounts occupy half the volume, and the total pressure doubles.

questions.stem: Argon, an unreactive gas, is added to 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at equilibrium in a rigid sealed vessel at constant temperature. What happens?
options: The position shifts right, because the total pressure has increased
The position shifts left, because argon dilutes the reacting gases
The position shifts right, because argon collides with SO₂ and O₂
The position does not change, because no reacting concentration changes
questions.explanation: The total pressure rises, but the amounts and volume, and so the concentrations, of SO₂, O₂ and SO₃ are unchanged. Q still equals Keq, so there is no shift; a pressure change shifts an equilibrium only when it changes the concentrations of the reacting gases.

questions.stem: In the Contact process, vanadium(V) oxide is used as a catalyst for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). How does it help production?
options: Equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium yield is unchanged
The equilibrium yield of SO₃ increases, but the rate is unchanged
The forward reaction speeds up while the reverse reaction slows down
The reaction becomes endothermic, so a higher temperature can be used
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position and Keq are unchanged. This lets the plant run at a temperature where the rate would otherwise be too slow.

questions.stem: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) is at equilibrium. The solution is diluted with an equal volume of water. Which statement is correct?
options: Q stays equal to Keq, so the position does not change
Keq halves, so the system shifts left to a new position
Q becomes greater than Keq, so the system shifts left
Q becomes less than Keq, so the system shifts right
questions.explanation: Halving every concentration halves the numerator of Q and quarters its denominator, so Q becomes twice Keq. The system shifts left, towards the side with more particles in solution, until Q equals Keq again; Keq itself depends only on temperature.

questions.stem: In blood, haemoglobin binds oxygen: Hb + O₂ ⇌ HbO₂. At high altitude, where the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, what happens?
options: The equilibrium shifts left, because Keq falls at high altitude
The equilibrium shifts left, so less oxygenated haemoglobin forms
The equilibrium shifts right, so more oxygenated haemoglobin forms
The equilibrium does not shift, because Keq does not change
questions.explanation: A lower oxygen concentration shifts the equilibrium towards Hb and O₂, so less HbO₂ is carried to the tissues. Keq depends only on temperature, so the position changes but Keq does not; over time the body partly compensates by making more haemoglobin.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. Which set of methods increases the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
options: Using a lower pressure, a lower temperature and adding SO₃
Using excess air, a lower temperature and removing SO₃
Using excess air, a higher temperature and removing SO₃
Using a catalyst, a higher temperature and adding SO₃
questions.explanation: Extra oxygen and removing the product both shift the equilibrium right, and because the forward reaction is exothermic a lower temperature also favours SO₃. A catalyst changes only the rate, and a higher temperature lowers the yield of an exothermic reaction.

questions.stem: The Contact process gives a very high conversion of SO₂ to SO₃ at pressures only slightly above atmospheric. Why is a much higher pressure not used, even though it would favour SO₃?
options: A higher pressure would destroy the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst completely
The small gain in yield would not justify the cost of high-pressure equipment
A higher pressure would shift the equilibrium towards SO₂ and lower the yield
A higher pressure would make the forward reaction endothermic instead
questions.explanation: Higher pressure would shift the equilibrium further right, but the conversion is already very high, so the extra yield would be small compared with the cost of building and running high-pressure plant. Industrial conditions balance yield, rate and cost.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen leaving the reactor are recycled back into it. Why does this make production more economical?
options: Reactants that did not convert in one pass are not wasted
Recycling the gases increases the value of Keq for the reaction
Recycled gases are hotter, so the forward reaction becomes endothermic
Recycling removes the need for a catalyst in the reactor
questions.explanation: Only part of the gas mixture is converted to ammonia in each pass. Recycling the unreacted gases means that, over many passes, nearly all of the nitrogen and hydrogen end up as ammonia, which cuts raw material costs. Keq depends only on temperature.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?
options: Keq = [NO]²[O₂] / [NO₂]²
Keq = 2[NO₂] / (2[NO][O₂])
Keq = [NO₂] / ([NO][O₂])
Keq = [NO₂]² / ([NO]²[O₂])
questions.explanation: Product concentrations go on top and reactant concentrations below, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Coefficients become powers, not multipliers, so [NO₂] and [NO] are squared.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium expression for Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq)?
options: Keq = [FeSCN²⁺] / ([Fe³⁺] + [SCN⁻])
Keq = [FeSCN²⁺][Fe³⁺] / [SCN⁻]
Keq = [FeSCN²⁺] / ([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻])
Keq = [Fe³⁺][SCN⁻] / [FeSCN²⁺]
questions.explanation: The product concentration is divided by the product of the reactant concentrations, each with a power of 1 because all coefficients are 1. Reactant concentrations are multiplied, not added.

questions.stem: At 25 °C a reaction has Keq = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸. What does this indicate about the equilibrium mixture?
options: It reaches equilibrium very slowly
It reaches equilibrium very quickly
It contains mostly reactants
It contains mostly products
questions.explanation: A very small Keq means the numerator (products) is tiny compared with the denominator (reactants), so the position of equilibrium lies far to the left. Keq says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of Keq for a reaction?
options: Changing the temperature
Adding more of a reactant
Adding a suitable catalyst
Halving the vessel volume
questions.explanation: Keq is constant at a given temperature. Changing concentrations or volume moves the position of equilibrium without changing Keq, and a catalyst changes only how quickly equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: 1.00 mol of PCl₅ is placed in a sealed 2.00 L vessel. At equilibrium the vessel holds 0.40 mol of Cl₂. What is Keq for PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium n(PCl₃) = n(Cl₂) = 0.40 mol and n(PCl₅) = 1.00 − 0.40 = 0.60 mol. The concentrations are 0.20, 0.20 and 0.30 mol L⁻¹, so Keq = (0.20 × 0.20)/0.30 = 0.13. Using amounts in mol instead of concentrations gives 0.27.

questions.stem: Solutions are mixed so that initially [Fe³⁺] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ and [SCN⁻] = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Colorimetry shows [FeSCN²⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ at equilibrium. What is Keq for Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺?
questions.explanation: Forming 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ of FeSCN²⁺ uses the same amount of each reactant, leaving [Fe³⁺] = 1.90 × 10⁻³ and [SCN⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Keq = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ / (1.90 × 10⁻³ × 1.00 × 10⁻⁴) = 5.3 × 10². Leaving [Fe³⁺] at its initial value gives 5.0 × 10².

questions.stem: At a certain temperature Keq = 64 for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What is Keq for 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g) at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: Reversing an equation inverts its equilibrium expression, so the new Keq is 1/64 = 0.016. The value 0.13 is 1/8, which would apply to HI(g) ⇌ ½H₂(g) + ½I₂(g), where the coefficients have also been halved.

questions.stem: Keq = 49 for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at a certain temperature. At equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.020 mol L⁻¹. What is [HI]?
options: 0.020 mol L⁻¹
0.98 mol L⁻¹
0.28 mol L⁻¹
0.14 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Keq = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]), so [HI]² = 49 × 0.020 × 0.020 = 0.0196 and [HI] = 0.14 mol L⁻¹. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 0.0196, or about 0.020, and using 49 × 0.020 gives 0.98.

questions.stem: Keq = 0.20 for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at a certain temperature. A mixture has [N₂O₄] = 0.50 and [NO₂] = 0.50 mol L⁻¹. What happens as it moves to equilibrium?
options: Q = 0.50, which exceeds Keq, so NO₂ is converted to N₂O₄
Q = 0.50, which exceeds Keq, so N₂O₄ is converted to NO₂
Q = 1.0, which exceeds Keq, so N₂O₄ is converted to NO₂
Q = 2.0, which exceeds Keq, so NO₂ is converted to N₂O₄
questions.explanation: Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] = 0.25/0.50 = 0.50. Since Q is greater than Keq there is too much product, so the net reaction is in the reverse direction, converting NO₂ into N₂O₄ until Q falls to 0.20.

questions.stem: Keq = 49 for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). A mixture has [H₂] = 0.10, [I₂] = 0.10 and [HI] = 0.70 mol L⁻¹. Is it at equilibrium?
options: No; Q = 7.0, so the forward reaction is favoured
Yes, because Q = 49, which equals Keq
No; Q = 70, so the reverse reaction is favoured
No; Q = 0.020, so the forward reaction is favoured
questions.explanation: Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 0.49/0.010 = 49, which equals Keq, so the mixture is already at equilibrium and no net reaction occurs. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 70, and inverting the expression gives 0.020.

questions.stem: Keq for a gas-phase reaction is 4.3 at 300 K and 0.15 at 500 K. What does this show about the forward reaction?
options: It is endothermic, because Keq falls as temperature rises
It is exothermic, because the reaction is faster when hot
It is endothermic, because the reaction is slower when cold
It is exothermic, because Keq falls as temperature rises
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Keq falls on heating, so fewer products are present and the reverse reaction is the endothermic one, meaning the forward reaction is exothermic. Rate does not show whether a reaction is exothermic.

questions.stem: Keq for an endothermic reaction is 0.50 at 25 °C. What is its value at 50 °C?
options: Equal to 1.0, because Keq doubles when the temperature doubles
Greater than 0.50, because heating favours the forward reaction
Less than 0.50, because heating favours the reverse reaction
Equal to 0.50, because Keq does not depend on temperature
questions.explanation: For an endothermic forward reaction, heating shifts the equilibrium right, increasing the product concentrations relative to reactants, so Keq increases. There is no simple proportion between Celsius temperature and Keq.

questions.stem: In the practical to determine Keq for the iron(III) thiocyanate system, how is the equilibrium concentration of FeSCN²⁺ usually found?
options: By titrating the equilibrium mixture with sodium hydroxide
By measuring the volume of gas given off at equilibrium
By measuring the intensity of the red colour against standards
By weighing the FeSCN²⁺ that precipitates at equilibrium
questions.explanation: FeSCN²⁺ is the only strongly coloured species, so its concentration can be found from the colour intensity, using a colorimeter or by comparing with standard solutions. It does not precipitate or give off a gas, so weighing or gas volumes cannot be used.
